growth_story.headline: Norway's income per person grew 2.6 percent a year in 1990–2007, then 0.5 from 2008, while productivity growth slowed and oil and gas output passed its peak.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2007 Norway's income per person grew 2.6 percent a year. Since 2008 it has grown 0.5 percent a year, with falls of 2.8 percent in 2009 and 1.9 percent in 2020. Growth averaged 0.4 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 0.8 over 2016–2025, helped by a rebound of 3.6 in 2021 and 3.1 in 2022, but income per person fell 0.8 in 2023 and rose only 0.5 in 2024 and 0.4 in 2025. The sources point to productivity growth that has slowed for two decades and to oil and gas output that likely peaked as early as 2001; they also describe an oil price collapse in 2015 and an oil and gas price surge after Russia's invasion of Ukraine that lifted exports for a time. In 2025 income per person was at its highest yet, but only a little above the level it first reached in 2022.

threads.title: Oil and gas past their peak
threads.text: The OECD judges that Norway's oil and gas output likely peaked as early as 2001. Gas still moves the totals: the IMF says record gas extraction lifted total output in 2024.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe record gas extraction in 2024 and a pickup in the mainland economy in 2025, but income per person rose only 0.5 percent in 2024 and 0.4 in 2025. Several of the cited passages describe the mainland economy, without oil and gas, while the data cover the whole economy, oil and gas included, measured per person.
